brief.intro: A telecom tower or mast is a small-footprint, structure-led project whose real complexity is not size but precision: a steel lattice tower or monopole must be founded, erected plumb and earthed correctly, then equipped with antennas, feeders and a small equipment shelter. New to this type? Structural erection is quick once the foundation cures, so the programme is usually driven by access — a remote or difficult site, a tight access road — and by two testing gates that cannot be rushed: the plumbness/structural survey and the earthing/lightning-protection test. RF (radio-frequency) commissioning of the antennas and feeders is done last and is often on the telecom operator's own schedule, arriving after the tower itself is complete. Weather — wind limits for lifting, lightning risk during steel erection — is a frequent driver of float consumption on this type.

scope.name: Site access & enabling
scope.desc: Access road/track, site clearance and temporary power.

scope.name: Foundation & earth mat
scope.desc: Piled or spread foundation and a buried earth-electrode grid (earth mat).

scope.name: Tower / mast erection
scope.desc: Lattice tower sections or a monopole shaft, erected and plumbed.

scope.name: Equipment shelter / cabin
scope.desc: The base-station shelter housing radio and power equipment.

scope.name: Power supply
scope.desc: Utility connection or a solar/generator hybrid, DC power plant and battery backup.

scope.name: Earthing & lightning protection
scope.desc: Earth-mat bonding, down-conductors and surge protection.

scope.name: Antennas, feeders & RF equipment
scope.desc: Antenna mounts, feeder cable runs and radio units.

scope.name: Structural & earthing testing
scope.desc: Plumbness/structural survey, earth-resistance test and lightning-protection continuity test.

scope.name: RF commissioning & handover
scope.desc: Antenna alignment, RF testing, network integration and handover to the operator.

must_get_right: Treat site access as a schedule risk on its own — a remote or difficult site can govern the whole programme more than the steel erection itself.
Never skip or rush the earth-resistance and lightning-protection test — a failed result after the tower is erected and cabled means re-work at height.

Sequence RF commissioning realistically — it is usually run by the telecom operator on their own schedule, not the erection contractor's, so hand off with a clear interface date rather than assuming it follows immediately.
Watch wind and lightning-risk windows for lifting operations — steel erection at height is weather-gated and easily loses days.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule; because of the small activity count, the network is often modelled at a combined Level 3/4, calculated by F9 with total float kept ≥ 0.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and erection works run a standard 6-day week with lifting restricted to permitted wind-speed windows; steel erection stops during lightning risk. RF commissioning follows the operator's own working calendar, which may differ from the erection contractor's.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs site access → foundation & earth mat cure → tower/mast erection → shelter & power install → earthing bond → structural/earthing test → antenna & feeder install → RF commissioning → handover. On a remote site, access itself can be the longest single float-consuming activity.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The access road/track is available or built before foundation works; ground and geotechnical conditions are as per survey; the operator's RF equipment and commissioning team are available to the agreed interface date; wayleaves/land access are secured.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: Fabricated steel and specialist power/RF equipment are tracked as milestones:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Remote or difficult sites constrain crane and delivery access for tower sections; a small footprint limits laydown space; earthing and RF-certified trades are specialist and often shared across many sites in a rollout.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: access-road delay on remote sites, a failed earth-resistance test after erection, and RF commissioning slipping behind the operator's own programme. Contingency is held before erection (weather) and before the earthing/structural test.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1–2 to the client/operator; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4 for erection-day sequencing — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
